title: Gears and torque
summary: Build a gear train, count turns in versus turns out, and measure the force at the output with the spring scale to see the same trade a lever makes, now spinning.
materials: LEGO Technic gear set (8, 16 and 24-tooth gears, axles and beams)

figure.alt: A small eight-tooth driver gear meshes with a larger twenty-four-tooth driven gear. Each gear has a fixed-length arm sticking up from its axle, the input arm on the driver and the output arm on the driven gear, both the same length, used later to compare pulling force.

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop runs again: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: last week a lever traded distance for force with a straight push. Can a spinning machine make the same trade? A gear train is a lever bent into a circle.

Imagine: two gears meshed together, a small one and a large one. Turn the small one and the large one turns too, but not the same amount, and not with the same push.

Plan: build a beam with a fixed-length arm on both the input axle and the output axle, the same length on each, so any force comparison between them is fair. Sketch the gear train on graph paper: which gear is the driver, which is driven, and how many teeth each one has. Count the teeth yourself before trusting any label on the part.

figure.alt: A small eight-tooth gear turns three times for every one turn of the large twenty-four-tooth gear it drives, and the large gear's output arm can push about three times as hard as the small gear's input arm needed, since force and speed trade against the teeth ratio.

steps.title: Gear ratio: the same trade, now turning
steps.body:
Two meshed gears push on each other at the same point with the same force, tooth against tooth. What differs is how far that point sits from each gear's own centre, since a bigger gear has a bigger radius.

That difference is where the trade comes from. Turn a small 8-tooth gear driving a large 24-tooth gear. The large gear turns only a third as often, since it has three times as many teeth to fill for every turn of the small one. But with the same-length arm on each axle, the large gear's output arm can push about three times as hard as the small gear's input arm needed. That is because gear ratio equals the teeth ratio, 24 to 8, which is 3 to 1.

Nothing here comes free. The output turns slower for the very same reason it pushes harder. Teeth ratio in, force and speed swapped on the way out, in a perfect gear train with no friction eating any of it.

figure.alt: The input gear's arm is turned by hand while the output gear's arm holds the spring scale near its tip. The scale is pulled upward until it stalls the output from turning, and the force is read at that instant.

steps.title: Count turns, then stall the output
steps.body:
Build three gear pairs one at a time: an 8-tooth driving a 24-tooth, an 8-tooth driving a 16-tooth, and a 16-tooth driving a 16-tooth as a same-size control. Fix a beam of the same length to both the input axle and the output axle for every pair, so the arm length never changes.

For each pair, turn the input axle by hand exactly 3 full turns and count how many turns the output axle makes. Write both numbers down.

Then comes the stall test. Turn the input axle slowly and steadily. Meanwhile, a hand or a partner hooks the spring scale to the end of the output arm and pulls just hard enough to stop the output from turning. Read the newtons at the moment it stalls. Do this three times for each pair and use the middle reading.
checklist: Turns counted for at least two gear pairs, and the output turns roughly matched the teeth ratio
The arm length on the input and output axle was the same for every gear pair tested
Stall force measured with the spring scale for at least two gear pairs, read three times each
The 1-to-1 control pair turned the same amount both ways, both close to equal force

steps.title: Gear ratio versus turns and force
steps.body:
The arm length on both axles and how steadily you turn the crank stay the same for every row. Only the gear pair changes.

Test three gear pairs, three runs each, nine rows in total. For each run, write the gear pair, the output turns for exactly 3 input turns, and the stall force in newtons at the output arm.
steps.question: Which gear pair needed the most stall force at the output, and about how many times more than the 1-to-1 pair?

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body: One line for each surprise. Classics this week: a gear pair that skips teeth under load instead of stalling cleanly, and an axle that slips inside its gear instead of turning it. Turning the crank at an uneven speed also makes the stall reading jump around more than the gear ratio explains.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photo of the 8-tooth to 24-tooth gear pair with both arms attached and the spring scale hooked at the stall point, next to your graph paper sketch with the teeth counts and all nine readings
